Payments were designed for people: sign up, enter a card, accept terms. An #AI agent can't do any of that. 🤖

paragraphs: In an announcement on Wednesday, the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative. With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites.

The FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satellite milestone by 2040. The FCC also deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits, rather than having them burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, saying the company hasn’t provided “sufficient information” about its disposal process plans.

SpaceX has described its Starmind project as a way to “capture solar energy in space to power” AI capabilities on Earth. The company says Starmind will transmit data to Earth using high-speed lasers that connect to Starlink. It plans to produce chips for its satellites at an upcoming Terafab facility.

Google has already taken its first steps toward putting compute into space, with the launch of a “Project Suncatcher” AI server satellite last month. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher in 2029.

paragraphs: The FCC on Wednesday granted the first authorization ever for a constellation of data centers in space — a win for Elon Musk and his SpaceX operation that comes less than two years after his role as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency under President Trump.
The authorization sees the Commission approve SpaceX’s deployment of 1 million orbital compute modules “to process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth.”
And, the Carr Commission proclaims, “it promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization—one that can harness the full power of the sun.”
The system also operates consistent with the FCC’s orbital debris rules.

In a statement, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said, “This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth. Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in SI. By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment. This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.”

With data centers a divisive topic across the U.S. in a wide range of communities, including Nashville, where a proposed center adjacent to the city’s zoo generated a vociferous round of protests in June, the idea of putting them in space could supercharge a company already seen by Wall Street as a potential disruptor to the cellular telephone industry. Already, T-Mobile has seen its stock price fall by $50 a share from earlier this year thanks to SpaceX efforts. On November 25, Microsoft shares were down to the low $480s after recently climbing above $500 per share.

paragraphs: Ask Dan Shipper how often venture-backed media startups succeed, and he’s candid.

“My feeling about the history of media companies taking venture capital is that it doesn’t go very well,” he said. In other words, it usually doesn’t work out, I suggest. “It works out never, actually,” laughs Shipper, founder of AI-focused media and software company Every.

Shipper’s right: VC-backed media startups of yesteryear have frequently tanked in spectacular fashion, from The Messenger and Vice to Ozy Media and Quibi. But Shipper is betting that Every—currently with about 130,000 unpaid subscribers and almost 10,000 paid—can play by its own rules and ultimately win its own game.

Hence, the fundraise: Every recently raised $17.5 million in Series A funding, at a $110 million post-money valuation, Fortune has exclusively learned. IA Ventures’s Jesse Beyroutey led the round, with Betaworks and The Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson joining, among others. Shipper, 35, will retain full control of the company, and is changing his title to “Philosopher King,” which I rib him about. He good-naturedly says the change is semiotic.

“The really important thing about taking the money for me was that we’d do it in a way that allows us to achieve our goals… and do it in a way that doesn’t require us to sacrifice our soul or the things about the company that I love deeply,” said Shipper. “I think of changing my title as a symbolic thing. If this was a normal venture capital deal, that would be completely off the table and ridiculous.”

And this isn’t a normal venture deal, in a couple of ways. First, Every is a media company. With its neoclassical pop art aesthetic, Every has a multi-pronged business model: Its writing serves a professional audience seeking to become “AI-native,” while the 35-person company also provides consulting services to large companies and produces conferences (I recently interviewed Shipper at Every’s Thesis: 2027 conference in Brooklyn). Second, Shipper didn’t raise in a standard startup process: IA’s Beyroutey and Shipper are close friends (they went to college together) and Shipper went straight to Beyroutey.

“I didn’t shop the deal,” said Shipper. “I went to someone I deeply trust, who understands the business deeply, who understands exactly what I want to do with it, and has put me in the position where I make all the decisions to build the company in the way that I want to build it,” Shipper said. “I think that’s the only way to build a business like this, because this is a very unique shape. It’s a media company and a technology company, kind of smushed together.”

Shipper started Every in 2020, about six years after exiting his first startup, co-browsing company Firefly, in 2014 (the acquisition came right as he was graduating college). He spent the intervening years finding the right next thing. Every became the answer, in part because it addressed a number of questions that Shipper had been asking throughout his life. For one, he’d long felt tension between writing and entrepreneurship (at Every he could be both). He’d also been interested in tech since he was a kid.

“I thought a lot about why Microsoft and Windows had worked, and one of the big reasons is that they came during a hardware platform shift, from mainframes to PCs,” said Shipper. “They started building operating systems for that, and that’s always a really big opportunity…. And I thought: I wonder what my platform shift is going to be?”
Shipper and Every are all-in on AI, and the company is built to help people understand how they can actually use AI, in their jobs and their lives.

“I think too few companies are trying to do that,” said Shipper. “Too many companies are trying to build the machine god or are worrying about Armageddon, and I’m not…. I would expect improvements we’re seeing [in AI] to continue, and I would expect there to be a gap between the improvements that you see on the charts and how well those improvements translate into actually better work by people (and that people at companies are proud of). Our job is to fill that gap.”
Shipper is optimistic that AI won’t replace humans at work, a common fear and feature of AI discourse.

news.title: Every raises $17.5 million at $110 million valuation, betting venture-backed media can work
news.title_en: Every raises $17.5 million at $110 million valuation, betting venture-backed media can work
news.author: Allie Garfinkle
news.summary_en:
Ask Dan Shipper how often venture-backed media startups succeed, and he’s candid.

“My feeling about the history of media companies taking venture capital is that it doesn’t go very well,” he said. In other words, it usually doesn’t work out, I suggest. “It works out never, actually,” laughs Shipper, founder of AI-focused media and software company Every.

paragraphs: Ask Dan Shipper how often venture-backed media startups succeed, and he’s candid.

“My feeling about the history of media companies taking venture capital is that it doesn’t go very well,” he said. In other words, it usually doesn’t work out, I suggest. “It works out never, actually,” laughs Shipper, founder of AI-focused media and software company Every.

Shipper’s right: VC-backed media startups of yesteryear have frequently tanked in spectacular fashion, from The Messenger and Vice to Ozy Media and Quibi. But Shipper is betting that Every—currently with about 130,000 unpaid subscribers and almost 10,000 paid—can play by its own rules and ultimately win its own game.

Hence, the fundraise: Every recently raised $17.5 million in Series A funding, at a $110 million post-money valuation, Fortune has exclusively learned. IA Ventures’s Jesse Beyroutey led the round, with Betaworks and The Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson joining, among others. Shipper, 35, will retain full control of the company, and is changing his title to “Philosopher King,” which I rib him about. He good-naturedly says the change is semiotic.

“The really important thing about taking the money for me was that we’d do it in a way that allows us to achieve our goals… and do it in a way that doesn’t require us to sacrifice our soul or the things about the company that I love deeply,” said Shipper. “I think of changing my title as a symbolic thing. If this was a normal venture capital deal, that would be completely off the table and ridiculous.”

And this isn’t a normal venture deal, in a couple of ways. First, Every is a media company. With its neoclassical pop art aesthetic, Every has a multi-pronged business model: Its writing serves a professional audience seeking to become “AI-native,” while the 35-person company also provides consulting services to large companies and produces conferences (I recently interviewed Shipper at Every’s Thesis: 2027 conference in Brooklyn). Second, Shipper didn’t raise in a standard startup process: IA’s Beyroutey and Shipper are close friends (they went to college together) and Shipper went straight to Beyroutey.

“I didn’t shop the deal,” said Shipper. “I went to someone I deeply trust, who understands the business deeply, who understands exactly what I want to do with it, and has put me in the position where I make all the decisions to build the company in the way that I want to build it,” Shipper said. “I think that’s the only way to build a business like this, because this is a very unique shape. It’s a media company and a technology company, kind of smushed together.”

Shipper started Every in 2020, about six years after exiting his first startup, co-browsing company Firefly, in 2014 (the acquisition came right as he was graduating college). He spent the intervening years finding the right next thing. Every became the answer, in part because it addressed a number of questions that Shipper had been asking throughout his life. For one, he’d long felt tension between writing and entrepreneurship (at Every he could be both). He’d also been interested in tech since he was a kid.

“I thought a lot about why Microsoft and Windows had worked, and one of the big reasons is that they came during a hardware platform shift, from mainframes to PCs,” said Shipper. “They started building operating systems for that, and that’s always a really big opportunity…. And I thought: I wonder what my platform shift is going to be?”
Shipper and Every are all-in on AI, and the company is built to help people understand how they can actually use AI, in their jobs and their lives.

“I think too few companies are trying to do that,” said Shipper. “Too many companies are trying to build the machine god or are worrying about Armageddon, and I’m not…. I would expect improvements we’re seeing [in AI] to continue, and I would expect there to be a gap between the improvements that you see on the charts and how well those improvements translate into actually better work by people (and that people at companies are proud of). Our job is to fill that gap.”
Shipper is optimistic that AI won’t replace humans at work, a common fear and feature of AI discourse.

news.title: FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space
news.title_en: FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space
news.author: Emma Roth
news.summary_en:
In an announcement on Wednesday, the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative. With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites.

The FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satel
paragraphs: In an announcement on Wednesday, the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative. With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites.

The FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satellite milestone by 2040. The FCC also deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits, rather than having them burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, saying the company hasn’t provided “sufficient information” about its disposal process plans.

SpaceX has described its Starmind project as a way to “capture solar energy in space to power” AI capabilities on Earth. The company says Starmind will transmit data to Earth using high-speed lasers that connect to Starlink. It plans to produce chips for its satellites at an upcoming Terafab facility.

Google has already taken its first steps toward putting compute into space, with the launch of a “Project Suncatcher” AI server satellite last month. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher in 2029.

paragraphs: The FCC on Wednesday granted the first authorization ever for a constellation of data centers in space — a win for Elon Musk and his SpaceX operation that comes less than two years after his role as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency under President Trump.
The authorization sees the Commission approve SpaceX’s deployment of 1 million orbital compute modules “to process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth.”
And, the Carr Commission proclaims, “it promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization—one that can harness the full power of the sun.”
The system also operates consistent with the FCC’s orbital debris rules.

In a statement, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said, “This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth. Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in SI. By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment. This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.”

With data centers a divisive topic across the U.S. in a wide range of communities, including Nashville, where a proposed center adjacent to the city’s zoo generated a vociferous round of protests in June, the idea of putting them in space could supercharge a company already seen by Wall Street as a potential disruptor to the cellular telephone industry. Already, T-Mobile has seen its stock price fall by $50 a share from earlier this year thanks to SpaceX efforts. On November 25, Microsoft shares were down to the low $480s after recently climbing above $500 per share.

paragraphs: Many problems have a generator–verifier gap: it’s often far easier to verify that a solution is correct than to come up with one. Sudoku is a classic example. It’s simple to check the solution (just count the numbers in each row, column, and box), but finding that solution can take a long time. Many ambitious Claude projects have relied on this gap: formalizing proofs in mathematics or migrating large, well-tested codebases are tasks Claude can take on as long as it has a reliable way to verify its work.

But as Claude has become more capable, it’s begun to take on projects in live systems, where generating the work is easier than verifying it. In these systems, users often rely on edge cases and quirks that fall outside the test suite, and it’s hard to write a definition of “correct” that covers everything. Without a reliable way to check Claude’s work, the migration of a live system is hard to trust—however quickly Claude can generate the code for it.

We ran into this problem when we migrated our Messages API from Python to Rust. This API is the primary way that customers—as well as our own apps, like Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude. From early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times. Rust would allow us to use far less CPU per request. Claude wrote a first version of the API’s core request path in about a week. But building trust in the migration required us to find a way to verify that our Rust API was at parity with our production API. This proved hard for several reasons, including that the Python API continued changing throughout the migration, so parity was a moving target; Claude can reply nondeterministically to the same request, so a difference between two outputs didn’t necessarily mean a bug; and we couldn't read customer requests, so we weren't able to easily see where the two versions diverged.

In this post, we share how we turned the production Messages API itself into a verifier—and how that helped us test the new Rust version on production traffic, find where it differed, and automatically dispatch agents to fix those differences. This allowed us to ship an API on Rust that uses about 70% less CPU per request and cuts median time to first token by about 20% without ever taking the service offline or freezing feature development.
### Why migrate?

We built the Messages API in 2023 and wrote it in Python, which was widely used internally for much of our research code. At first, it was simple. The Messages API passed requests to the model and sent back what the model wrote. (One engineer at the time called it “basically a request forwarder.”) But as the Messages API became more capable and deeply integrated with our codebases, it also developed shared dependencies with Python libraries that were owned by our research and inference teams, which made it hard to move. If we ever wanted to move to another language, it would mean building logging, metrics, and tools all over again.

This calculus gradually began to change. By late 2025, every Messages API request had to be validated, converted into the prompt, tokenized, and screened by our safety classifiers. As each reply arrived, the stream of tokens had to be sorted into text, thinking, and tool calls, and Python added overhead to every one of those steps each time it created an object, freed memory, or handed its work to the next task. Traffic eventually grew far beyond what the initial Python service was built for (Figure 1), and we quickly needed to find a way to make the service much more efficient.
#### Incremental or all at once?

Full rewrites of large production systems are often approached cautiously, for at least two reasons. First, there is no guarantee that test suites cover 100% of production code behavior, and rewriting it is risky. Second, the sheer effort required often makes such work intractable. (In 2024, after one of our engineers suggested migrating to Go or Rust, another temporarily settled the question: “We are not rewriting the API in go or rust!”)

The standard advice if you’re looking for performance gains is thus to rewrite only the parts that are slowing the system down, so that’s where we started. In Rust, we rewrote the code that parses a model’s output and called it from Python. This reduced the API’s CPU usage by about 8% to 10%. However, incremental solutions often incur added complexity, and it’s important to make sure that incremental improvements justify those costs. In our case, the gains didn’t justify the added complexity. Each token now crossed between Python and Rust three times (Figure 2), creating new sources of overhead.

As Claude became increasingly capable, we began to question whether the usual reasons to avoid a full migration still held. The effort required to undertake the project was dropping fast: by May 2026, Claude was writing more than 80% of the code Anthropic merged. We wondered if Claude could now help us write code that would empirically capture every behavior and fix in the production system. But the question became: how could we verify that the behavior of our migration was correct? Verification, not generation, had become the bottleneck.

news.title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
news.title_en: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
news.author: Casey Crownhart
news.summary_en:
In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just on
paragraphs: In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10 . And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants . How did we get here?

If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today.

But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants.

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher , an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.

This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report . That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google ( 18% ), Amazon ( 16% ), and Microsoft ( 25% ). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there.

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation.

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead.

It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source.

But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025.

paragraphs: Amazon and Meta are in talks to end the block on Meta's AI shopping agent Muse in Amazon's online store. In September, Amazon blocked Muse's access. Ad revenue and control over search results are the main sticking points in the ongoing talks, Fortune reports. Amazon worries that shopping agents like Muse could weaken its relationship with customers and bypass the ads on its platform, a business that brings in $68.6 billion a year.

Andy Jassy, Amazon's CEO, said shopping through third-party agents so far hasn't been more convenient or better than going directly to a retailer, but he didn't rule out opening access. The company also offers its own agentic shopping features, which in some cases have pulled in sellers that don't sell on Amazon. It previously tried and failed to block Perplexity. Any deal would need sign-off from both CEOs, according to Fortune.

Muse is Meta's most successful consumer AI product so far, with more than 10 million users in the US and Canada. Meta is already seeing gains in its Instagram ad business because Muse helps users organize saved products, which boosts conversion rates for advertisers, CNBC reports. Data from Forter Intelligence shows that Muse recently accounted for 51 percent of all agentic orders, followed by SpaceX's Grok at 24 percent and OpenAI's ChatGPT at 22 percent.

paragraphs: Nothing is showing off a much more detailed look at its upcoming AI earbuds ahead of their December 8th release. The Ear Note buds can record your calls, while their charging case can record, transcribe, and summarize your conversations.

Like the Ear 3, the Ear Note’s microphone-equipped case comes with a “Talk” button that you can use to record your own voice. There’s also a new “Record” button that can record and transcribe your conversations. In a post on X, Nothing CEO Carl Pei says the button will allow you to record calls through the earbuds, and meetings through the case as a “first step toward a hardware context layer for AI.”

As previously reported by Bloomberg, the buds will connect to an app where you can manage recordings, transcriptions, and AI summaries. They’ll also “support interactions with various AI agents, including a more basic voice-control system developed by Nothing, letting users engage in back-and-forth conversations,” according to Bloomberg.

The Ear Note buds themselves look similar to the Ear 3 and Ear 3A, but come with Nothing’s “best in-ear audio to date.” The new device, which Nothing teased earlier this month, will join some of the other AI-powered note-taking devices we’ve seen emerge recently, such as the Amazon Bee and the Plaud Note Pro. Apple also brought AI capabilities to its Watch Series 12, allowing Siri to listen to your conversations and generate recaps.

news.title: US stocks sell-off deepens as AI trade cracks
news.title_en: US stocks sell-off deepens as AI trade cracks
news.author: Emily Herbert, Ian Smith, and William Sandlund
news.summary_en: Tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 falls more than 4% as weeks-long slide continues — A Wall Street sell-off intensified on Wednesday …
paragraphs: A Wall Street sell-off intensified on Wednesday, pushing the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 down more than 4 per cent, as a brutal unwind of the once-dominant AI trade accelerated.

Shares in Nvidia, which soared on Monday following the shock reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive, slid as much as 9 per cent. Rival chipmaker Broadcom lost 7 per cent, while Micron was down 11 per cent.
“The mood is extremely skittish,” said Van Luu, director of global solutions strategy at Russell Investments.

The euphoria sparked by Huang’s return to the top job at Nvidia, America’s biggest chipmaker and the face of the AI boom, had been replaced by a growing realisation “that the scrutiny on the AI ecosystem will [now] intensify”, he added.
The falls briefly pushed the Nasdaq back into a bear market, defined as a fall of 20 per cent from a recent high.
Shares in Claude maker Anthropic, which fell below their $83 listing price for the first time on Tuesday, dropped another 9 per cent on Wednesday to just under $75 as the slump deepened.
In early trading, Anthropic’s market valuation dipped below $1tn for the first time since its listing.
The weakness in tech stocks extends a weeks-long sell-off as doubts mount over whether the historic AI-driven spending boom will pay off and how it will be financed amid climbing interest rates.
In a sign of the souring in risk appetite, traders bought into low-risk US government debt on Wednesday, pushing the 10-year bond yield down 0.08 percentage points to 4.82 per cent.
The Vix index of expected volatility, Wall Street’s so-called fear gauge, remained elevated at above 35 points, more than double its September low.
“It’s pretty wild out there at the moment,” said Jim Reid, global head of macro research at Deutsche Bank, saying the “risk-off” mood in markets was further stoked by the latest tariff headlines.
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday unveiled a number of new tariffs on major trading partners, including the EU, China, Japan and South Korea.

paragraphs: Amazon has held talks about letting Meta’s Muse AI agent shop on its online marketplace, according to a report from Fortune. The discussions, which could end Amazon’s block on Muse, reportedly center on the kinds of products the AI agent recommends and the potential impact on the ecommerce giant’s advertising revenue.

As reported by Fortune, Amazon is concerned that it could lose advertising revenue by allowing Muse on its site, since it depends on actual humans seeing ads across its online marketplace. It’s also reportedly worried about the quality of the product search results that Muse will present to users, as well as whether the AI agent will affect Amazon’s relationship with customers. Neither Amazon nor Meta immediately responded to The Verge’s request for comment.

Though some online retailers, such as Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, and Sephora, have opened their digital doors to AI agents like Muse, Amazon has been more hesitant. Amazon also blocked Perplexity’s AI agent from shopping on its site, and has instead focused on promoting its own Alexa for Shopping assistant, which customers can now text to shop on their behalf.

This action marks a significant shift as the two issuers utilized centralized control over their smart contracts to execute immediate asset blocks upon requests from government authorities and the affected exchange.
paragraphs: As North Korean cyberthieves were funneling billions out of Binance last month, the world’s largest crypto exchange looked to two other companies to help stop the bleeding: Tether and Circle.

The duo, which issue cryptocurrencies that mimic the US dollar, reacted unusually quickly to freeze accounts hackers were using to move their haul around. It was a sign of the seriousness of the hack, the industry’s maturation, and the most public showcasing yet of the near-total control Tether and Circle exert over the tokens they created. They dominate the market, with their two main stablecoins together representing 86% of all in circulation.

As the $6.3 billion Binance hack was unfolding, Tether froze more than $1.5 billion of its USDT coin in 30 minutes, while Circle froze $1.1 billion of its USDC. Their swift actions – prompted by requests from Binance as well as the US government — became a tourniquet for what would otherwise have been a much more severe and expensive heist.

Until now, Tether and Circle have largely had different approaches to freezing, which essentially means blocking movement to and from specific addresses on blockchain networks that shift crypto around.

Tether has been criticized for not having a consistent modus operandi, sometimes allowing tokens to slide away unimpeded and other times seizing them indefinitely. It sometimes charges a fee to eventually return them, according to customers who described their experiences. Meanwhile, Circle’s philosophy until recently had been to only act after receiving a court order, a method so structured and time-consuming that the judge’s decision could be irrelevant by the time it came.

But during the Binance cybertheft, both companies acted almost immediately — in a fashion Circle referred to as “machine speed.” Luckily for Binance, which owns a stake in Circle, the company took a different tack than in some prior hacking episodes. Back in May, it also changed a policy stated on its website to only require a legal order from a government authority rather than from a court.
A spokesperson said this language change reflected “longstanding practice.”

Binance also temporarily halted withdrawals and fully restored stolen assets to customers’ accounts at its own expense, marking a relative success for crypto investors who might otherwise be suffering losses or left in limbo. Yet the speed of the Binance response stands in contrast to the experience of victims of earlier hacks, some of whom have spent years trying to recover frozen funds.

Take Bittok Technology Pte. Ltd., a small Singaporean crypto exchange that lost $50 million to hackers in June 2020. Tether decided to freeze some of the assets. But after more than five years, none of Bittok’s USDT had been returned after a circuitous path through attorney wrangling.

Along the way, a lawyer representing Tether advised the entity that acquired Bittok about a 20% “reissuance fee” on whatever was returned, according to emails reviewed by Bloomberg News. It’s not the only time Tether has done so: in several instances, victims only received their stolen USDT in chunks over time, with the same kind of fee, according to people involved who did not want to be identified because the negotiations were private.

Berlin-based Valentyn Golyshenko pleaded for help online for months from Tether, regulators and politicians after getting caught in a $75,000 scam, according to his social-media posts. In his telling, requests to freeze funds were rejected, and ultimately the wallet holding his pilfered crypto was drained to zero. Tether Chief Executive Officer Paolo Ardoino appears to have blocked him, and Golyshenko recently made his X account private.
In Circle’s case, the company has mostly been accused of being too prescriptive.

news.summary_en: Google DeepMind VP of Research Koray Kavukcuoglu announced that AI agents now manage partial compute for Gemini experiments, transitioning from project-specific teams to a unified general-purpose algorithm architecture. This shift aims to accelerate iteration cycles while preventing recursive self-improvement to maintain human-verifiable control over model reasoning.
paragraphs: Google Deepmind lets AI agents run experiments on their own for the next Gemini model. On the company's podcast, VP of Research Koray Kavukcuoglu, who leads Gemini development, frames this as part of a strategic shift at the lab. Rather than running separate teams for specialized projects like AlphaFold and nuclear fusion, Deepmind now relies on a single general-purpose algorithm for both science and products, he says. Each Gemini generation, he adds, is a hand-built one-off rather than a fixed architecture, while parallel teams work on its successors.

According to Kavukcuoglu, AI agents control part of the compute themselves to run experiments, though the lab is still far from full recursive self-improvement. As a safety measure, Deepmind doesn't reward the agents' internal thought streams ("Chain of Thought") during training, he says, so their intentions stay unfiltered and reviewable in natural language before they act.

Kavukcuoglu also points to limits. Today's AI can depict physical processes such as fluid flows and collisions with visual accuracy, he says, but doesn't understand them precisely. No test can show when models will close those gaps and reach artificial general intelligence (AGI), he argues, because no benchmark captures the core of intelligence. In his view, AGI won't begin until useful everyday products earn enough trust for people to hand decisions over to them, the way they would when working with other people.

news.summary_en:

paragraphs: AI models keep getting better, but putting them to work mostly creates friction, a new Anthropic report finds. Review bottlenecks, employee pushback, security risks, and outdated custom tools are dragging down many enterprise projects.

Anthropic's researchers conducted 66 in-person interviews at 58 US companies for the qualitative study, from AI startups to established firms in law, construction, finance, medicine, and manufacturing. The authors note that the sample isn't representative because every participant is an Anthropic customer. Still, it offers a detailed look at nearly 300 real-world AI deployments.

The findings from the "Working with AI"report amount to a reality check for anyone expecting quick efficiency gains. Respondents say 55 percent of the deployments studied produced higher output or better quality. But almost one in five (19 percent) still delivers no business value. Those deployments get stuck in internal bottlenecks (6 percent), lose their time savings to review work (5 percent), or have unclear effects (8 percent).
External hurdles like regulation (4 mentions) and skeptical customers (13 mentions) barely came up. The real pain happens inside the companies themselves, according to the report.
### AI output overwhelms reviewers and sparks workplace friction

The most common obstacle cited in Anthropic's full report (PDF) is the volume of AI output that humans still need to check (49 mentions). Employee resistance (43 mentions) and required expert reviews and testing (42 mentions) rank close behind. In one case, an AI agent added one stray "S"to an API call and derailed a carefully planned software release.

AI also tends to speed up only parts of a workflow while other departments fall behind (20 mentions). One industrial equipment maker found that AI could translate its product interface text into 10 languages with ease. The company shut the feature back down because nobody on staff could field customer support calls in those languages.

That uneven pace breeds day-to-day conflict as power users flood coworkers with AI-generated text. The report mentions "Claude grenades"and "Claude cannons,"as when an employee casually sends IT seven pages of AI-written instructions.
Skeptics push back and refuse to read AI-written emails at all. One frustrated executive put it bluntly, saying, "A mediocre engineer with an AI is a menace to society."

Anthropic's findings echo the broader "workslop"debate. In a survey by BetterUp Labs and the Stanford Social Media Lab, 40 percent of US workers said they regularly receive shallow AI content from colleagues. Workers spend an average of nearly two hours dealing with each incident, and the survey found that trust within teams takes a hit.
### Job fears drive quiet resistance among employees
Employee resistance is the second most common obstacle in Anthropic's study, with 43 mentions. Pushback is most visible when companies roll out AI from the top down to automate entire workflows.

paragraphs: The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) took systems offline as a precaution after unauthorized access. Hours earlier, reports emerged of a separate breach at the CIA and other US intelligence agencies that may have involved an AI tool.
FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident. The Verge reported that the agency announced on Tuesday that a limited portion of its systems had been accessed without authorization.

While FinCEN didn't disclose the scope or cause of the incident, it took some systems offline as a precaution. FinCEN's mission is to protect the financial system from illegal activity such as money laundering and terrorist financing. It also manages financial transaction data for law enforcement and collects suspicious activity reports from banks under the Bank Secrecy Act.
Banks can still file suspicious activity reports online, FinCEN says, though some services may face delays. Its telephone hotline for financial institutions isn't affected, the agency says.
### Separate breach hits US spy agencies' open-source intelligence system

The New York Times reported a breach at several US intelligence agencies just hours before FinCEN's announcement, citing US officials and others familiar with the matter. According to the Times, the intrusion hit the CIA, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA), and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI).

The report said intruders broke into an analysis system for open-source intelligence that searches publicly available, unclassified information to produce intelligence. That includes commercially available datasets, social media content, satellite imagery, and other online material, according to the report. Even though much of this data is freely available or sold by data brokers, it can be revealing when combined, the Times noted.

It's still not clear what specific data was accessed or taken. Classified information wasn't at risk, sources told the Times. One person familiar with the matter said the issue has since been resolved, and an ODNI representative said critical capabilities weren't affected.
### Attackers may have used Artex, a repurposed AI defense tool

Multiple sources told the New York Times that investigators suspect the attackers behind the intelligence breach used Artex, an AI hacking tool. A Chinese engineer released the tool in July to help organizations defend against cyberattacks. US officials and security experts say attackers have since repurposed it for offensive use.

Cybersecurity researchers have linked Artex to dozens of attacks on companies worldwide since its release, including in Japan and South Korea. Investigators haven't yet determined who was behind the US intelligence breach. Early indicators, including the use of Artex, point to possible Chinese involvement, according to two people familiar with the matter. Western officials have accused Chinese intelligence services and a network of contractors of cyberattacks on US agencies and companies for years, allegations Beijing routinely denies.
### A string of federal hacks and outages has left the US public uneasy

This open defiance of U.S. export controls is in evidence in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, just a few miles from the state villa where President Donald Trump met Chinese leader Xi Jinping last week and hailed him as a “friend.”
During a recent visit, one vendor in a corner of Huaqiangbei at first denied that he knew where to find high-end Nvidia chips. Then, he relented.
The day's top stories, curated by Washington Post editors. Sign up for free
After making a few calls to suppliers, he quoted a price of 20 million renminbi — around $3 million — for a server containing eight Blackwell B300s, the most advanced Nvidia chips produced.

The traders of Huaqiangbei form part of a vast effort in China to secure vaunted Nvidia chips and keep up with the United States, which China lags in the artificial intelligence race. In recent weeks, that effort has only grown more urgent as the U.S. tightens its export controls following an alleged Chinese espionage plot targeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who was forced by his board to step down before a whiplash return on Monday.

In a sign that their supply networks are coming under strain from the fast-moving events in the U.S., Huaqiangbei vendors said that the prices of Nvidia chips have risen drastically in the past few weeks.

Two months ago, a Blackwell B300 server was priced at just $2 million, according to Wu, a vendor who spoke on the condition that he be identified only by his last name for fear of official scrutiny. “If U.S. authorities or Nvidia restrict the supply, the price will rise,” Wu said. “But of course, after a certain point, the demand will be very low. It’s not good for our business.”

Nvidia does not publicly disclose prices for its high-end chips, but an equivalent B300 server retails for roughly $500,000 to $600,000 in the U.S., said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, a Washington think tank.

The prices in Huaqiangbei, which fluctuate as market conditions change, illustrate a complex and ever-evolving battle between Beijing, Washington and Nvidia to widen or narrow the supply of U.S. chips available to China.
Nvidia chips are the “decisive factor” in the AI competition between the U.S. and China, Chan said. “Who can get access to the best Nvidia chips matters tremendously.”
Finding U.S.-restricted Nvidia chips to buy in Shenzhen is simply a matter of asking the right person.

news.title: Has vibe coding made open source the new normal for synths?
news.title_en: Has vibe coding made open source the new normal for synths?
news.author: Terrence O'Brien
news.summary_en:
The emergence of powerful vibe-coding agents and tools like Reverse Engineer Anything has caused chaos in the music gear world, leaving companies scrambling to figure out how to respond. While some, like Roland, have remained silent for now, others have embraced the modding community. Th
paragraphs: The emergence of powerful vibe-coding agents and tools like Reverse Engineer Anything has caused chaos in the music gear world, leaving companies scrambling to figure out how to respond. While some, like Roland, have remained silent for now, others have embraced the modding community. In the last several weeks, as it’s become clear that no piece of music gear is safe from Claude and a subreddit full of curious tinkerers, companies have begun making more and more of their devices open source.

The biggest name to decide “if you can’t beat ’em, join ’em” is inMusic, the parent company of Akai, Moog, Native Instruments, and more. “We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community, we’re going to provide the inner workings of, say, an MPC or Sample so that people can do what they want,” inMusic CEO Jack O’Donnell tells The Verge. That includes a recently launched SDK and several open-source devices, including the recently teased MPC Sample Key.

Akai is trying to walk a fine line, offering modders access while keeping its products reliable for professionals. O’Donnell says the company will “try to give them a reset button” so “they can experiment with it, and then not lose what they have.”

Behringer has also rushed to cash in, announcing a slew of open-source devices. In just a matter of weeks, it announced a $150 clone of the MPC One called Kick, a clone of the E-mu SP-1200, the Anima DJ controller, the Ignite sequencer, and the Polykeys 61 MIDI controller, all of which are open source. It’s unclear when any of these products might launch.

M-Vave’s FM-1 helped kick-start the whole movement. The $70 pocketable clone of the iconic Yamaha DX7 became the synth of the summer not just because of its dirt-cheap price and faithfully re-created ’80s tones, but because it also turned out to be infinitely hackable. There are well over a dozen different custom firmwares for the FM-1. M-Vave responded by releasing an open-source firmware with more features for developers to build on. The company also confirmed that a successor, the FM-2, is in development and will be open source as well.

Other companies have also embraced the modding community. Erica Synths recently released the source code for its LXR-02 drum machine, but founder Ģirts Ozoliņš isn’t necessarily fully on board with vibe coding. “Inventions succeed if they solve some fundamental problems, right?” he tells The Verge. “So, I’m still wondering what fundamental problem vibe coding solves.”
“We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community.”

While he can’t imagine a producer simply stacking his studio with a bunch of hacked FM-1s running various synth engines, he’s curious to see what the community cooks up for the LXR. And he does see a benefit in making music tech a little less disposable. “What I like on the upside of this is that there is some trace of sustainability. Instead of buying five or 10 plastic boxes, you can try options on one,” he says, though he’s under no illusions about the environmental impact of vibe coding. “Of course it by far does not offset data center impact on the planet and on ecology and stuff like that.”

Polyend has also gotten on board, open-sourcing its line of Tracker grooveboxes. The Polish company’s decision to open its arms to vibe coders isn’t too much of a surprise. Last year it released the Endless guitar pedal, which lets users vibe-code their own effects. Opening its other instruments to AI tinkering feels like a natural extension.

Elektron is less thrilled about the emergence of vibe-coded mods. The company banned links to custom firmware from its official forums, saying, “We would always warn against modifications to our firmware and/or machines that could brick them (potentially rendering them unusable), prevent future updates, affect warranty coverage.”

Elektron’s CPO Christian Alsing told YouTuber EZBOT that he was sympathetic to the hacker community and that the company has roots there with its first instrument, the Sidstation (based on the iconic SID sound chip from the Commodore 64). He also said that he believes users have a right to modify their devices as they see fit. But he pushed back on the idea that Elektron is “withholding features,” an accusation that Akai also faced.

Ģirts also defended Elektron, saying, “people tend to blame the company, saying they are hiding features ... you design an instrument, you have a specific concept in mind, and you cannot foresee millions of possibilities ... it’s not about hiding features; it’s more about having an idea of how an instrument should look and work.”

paragraphs: Walmart-backed fintech major PhonePe has revived its IPO plans and restarted discussions with investment bankers, targeting a March 2027 listing at a valuation of $12 Bn to $15 Bn, sources told Inc42.

The Bengaluru-based company plans to file updated IPO papers by December-end for an offer for sale of up to ₹12,000 Cr ($1.3 Bn). Notably, PhonePe was valued at $14.5 Bn during General Atlantic’s $600 Mn secondary investment in 2025. Sources said PhonePe expects greater clarity by December-end on two regulatory issues affecting the company’s business – the merchant discount rate (MDR) framework for UPI transactions and the 30% market-share cap for third-party UPI apps. A possible extension or relaxation of the cap could ease a regulatory overhang ahead of the proposed listing, the sources said. PhonePe declined to comment on the IPO development. The Economic Times first reported on the revival of its listing plans. The renewed push comes after PhonePe paused its IPO plans in March, citing geopolitical uncertainty and volatility in global capital markets. At the time, the company said it would restart the process once markets stabilised.
The rally in Indian equities and foreign portfolio investors’ return to net buying appear to have given PhonePe greater confidence to revive its listing plans.

PhonePe is seeing stronger growth in lending and operating revenue, the sources said. The company’s lending business has grown around 100%, while operating revenue has increased 35%-40% QoQ. The company is also expected to report a net profit, they added. This would mark a turnaround from FY26, when PhonePe reported a net loss of ₹2,792 Cr. Operating revenue rose 11.5% to ₹7,920.5 Cr from ₹7,105 Cr in FY25.

The lending business offers PhonePe a route to diversify revenue beyond its core payments operations. Its growth and contribution to profitability will be relevant to the company’s pitch to public market investors.
Beyond financial performance, the regulatory outlook remains central to PhonePe’s IPO preparations.
Introducing MDR on select UPI transactions could create an additional revenue stream for payment companies. However, whether such charges will be introduced remains uncertain.

The other issue is the National Payments Corporation of India’s (NPCI) 30% cap on UPI transaction volumes handled by individual third-party application providers (TPAPs). NPCI had extended the compliance deadline for existing apps exceeding the cap to December 31, 2026.
PhonePe operates above the threshold, making any further extension or relaxation significant for its growth plans ahead of the proposed public market debut.
Its renewed listing push also coincides with IPO preparations at payments infrastructure major Razorpay.

Razorpay has received SEBI’s approval for its proposed ₹5,000 Cr–₹6,000 Cr public offering. It is targeting a valuation of around $5 Bn (₹47,000 Cr), with a listing likely between January and March 2027, sources previously told Inc42. The timeline could put its debut ahead of PhonePe’s proposed March listing.

paragraphs: Startup PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an updated version of its aggressively compressed language model. It's based on Qwen3.8-27B and takes up just 5.9 GB of memory, same as its predecessor. That's possible because of ternary quantization, where each weight can only be one of three values (−1, 0, or +1) instead of the usual 16-bit storage. At full precision, a model this size would need about 54 GB.

Bonsai 2.5 is designed to perform more reliably on agentic tasks that involve long chains of tool calls. It needs fewer passes and tokens than Bonsai 2, and it's less likely to get stuck in loops or spiral into drawn-out reasoning phases.

The benchmark numbers reflect the improvement. On SWE-bench Verified, the score jumps from 60.8 to 75.6 percent. The full Qwen model hits 80.6. On AppWorld, an agent benchmark, Bonsai leaps from 51.2 to 90.5, landing just behind the base model. On LiveCodeBench v6, the new version scores slightly lower than its predecessor.

On an RTX 4090, the model generates about 204 tokens per second using multi-token prediction. The weights are available under an Apache 2.0 license and run via llama.cpp on Nvidia and Intel GPUs, as well as through MLX on Mac, iPhone, and iPad. PrismML grew out of a research team at Caltech and is backed by Khosla Ventures, Google, and Samsung, among others. The company first introduced Bonsai 27B in July, built on an older Qwen model. Its smallest variant needed less than 4 GB of memory, small enough to run directly on an iPhone.

news.title: ‘Rejection Will Have Consequences’: Inside Trump’s Demands to Another Chips CEO
news.title_en: ‘Rejection Will Have Consequences’: Inside Trump’s Demands to Another Chips CEO
news.author: Noah Shachtman
news.summary_en:
The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company. Right now. Or else.

Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms o
paragraphs: The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company. Right now. Or else.

Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms on Friday.”

Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors. But the Trump administration official “noted that rejection will have consequences that [Shapiro] cannot predict.”

Days later, the board gave the administration what it wanted. “It is my Great Honor to report that the United States of America now fully owns and controls 10% of INTEL,” Donald Trump posted to his social platform. “The United States paid nothing for these Shares, and the Shares are now valued at approximately $11 Billion Dollars. This is a great Deal for America.”

President Trump was similarly jubilant on Monday, announcing that he had “convinced” Nvidia’s board of directors to rehire chief executive Jensen Huang. The proclamation was a shock. But it wasn’t entirely without precedent.

Fifteen months earlier, the Trump administration had interfered with the leadership decisions at another major chipmaker, court documents allege. Then, as now, allegations swirled that the company’s CEO was too close to China. Then, as now, the Trump administration dealt itself into the company’s financial future.

It’s part of a broader shift within the government in general and the Commerce Department in particular, a former member of that department tells WIRED. Out are old metrics “like creating jobs or the US being more competitive or owning more of the market share,” this ex-Trump administration official says. When dealing with private companies, a single overriding concern is: “Are you going to give back to the government in cash?”

Documents unredacted as part of a shareholder’s lawsuit against Intel’s board show how far the administration has been willing to go to get what it wants. The lawsuit’s allegations were previously reported by WP Intelligence.

“The Board, operating under the shadow of the President’s threats,” the lawsuit alleges, “caved to the government’s extortion.” A second case, asking for internal records, was filed in April by the same shareholder, Richard Paisner, against Nvidia.

“It's just straight-up coercion,” says Scott Lincicome, a vice president at the libertarian Cato Institute. “The company starts making decisions not based on what's best for the company in the short or long term, what's best for shareholders, but what's best for politics and what the government is demanding.”

“That's not what you want from any company,” he adds. “When you're talking about the world's most innovative companies and these kinds of bleeding-edge technologies that have not only huge economic implications but national security ones, then that's a huge problem.”
Representatives for Intel declined to comment for this story. The White House, Commerce Department, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.

Huang, one of the most prominent figures in the AI industry, was reinstated by Nvidia's board on Monday in a reversal after Trump intervened on his behalf.
Trump told the Post that it was his understanding that Huang had not had affairs with other women linked to Beijing and that he did not know how many affairs Huang had acknowledged.
NVDA stock rallied 31.5% the same day, but the rally lost steam. Shares dipped nearly 6% in Tuesday's session and another 2.2% in overnight trading.
While Huang's return as Nvidia chief is a major shot in the arm for the company and the broader AI trade, some commentators say the AI chipmaker is not out of the woods yet.

news.title: Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long
news.title_en: Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long
news.author: Aarian Marshall
news.summary_en:

No
paragraphs: In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.

Da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations. Why, exactly, did water—any fluid, really, be it atmospheric air or blood in the heart—move in that way?

Now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works. “It’s the hardest remaining problem in classical physics, and it’s one we need to fly through,” says Michael Murillo, a professor of theoretical and computational physics at Michigan State University.

Now a bumper crop of data-driven efforts to predict and avoid turbulence could get fliers closer to a smooth flight. Twenty terabytes of data are created by an airplane’s engine in one hour of commercial flying, according to the International Air Transport Association, with more broadcast by airplanes midflight: GPS position, altitude, speed. An “electronic flight bag,” basically a specialized iPad, is equipped with navigation charts and manuals and can transmit its own information, as long as the airplane’s internet connection cooperates. Satellites watch and collect it all.

“Air traffic has gone up, and communication costs and the costs of putting computers on aircraft have come down,” says Larry Cornman, a physicist with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research who has been studying turbulence for decades. “The time is now to work on these things because we can do them.”

This is good news for aviation safety. More than 200 people were seriously injured on US airplanes in turbulence-related incidents between 2009 and 2023, according to FAA data. Turbulence is also getting worse. Climate change alters the atmospheric conditions around the world’s jet streams, creating destabilizing wind shear. From the cockpit of an airplane, this translates into sudden, clear-air turbulence, difficult to see or predict. Historically, pilots’ only method of avoiding turbulence is heeding the warning of those who accidentally went through it before them, and hoping that nothing had changed.

But just in the past two years, Cornman’s decades of work on turbulence has been put into the field in ways it couldn’t be before, part of several projects coordinated by the US federal government and the airline industry. One breakthrough came when Cornman and an FAA air traffic controller determined that aircrafts’ federally required broadcasts of their positions, altitude, and speed could be used to spot unexpected turbulence, without requiring new hardware or software onboard. Researchers can use this crowdsourced, public data to make predictions about when and where turbulence will pop up.

In September, the National Science Foundation announced a $30 million award to nine universities to stand up a new center dedicated to predicting turbulence—in the air, but also in the charged particles inside a fusion reactor, and in the gas clouds that stretch across space.

“Turbulence is the reason we don’t have fusion energy yet,” says Murillo, who heads up the new center, called Transformative Explorations in Multi-Physics and Engineering of Scientific Turbulence, or Tempest. The chaotic swirling of superhot plasma inside a reactor allows heat to leak out, preventing the material from reaching the temperatures needed to allow nuclei to fuse. The US federal government wants to get closer to figuring that out.

“Closer,” because turbulence is impossible to perfectly predict, scientists say. For one thing, turbulence occurs at many different, small scales at the same time. Air swirling around an airplane breaks into eddies, then smaller eddies, and then even smaller eddies, with each interacting with each other—too many variables, happening too quickly, to mathematically account for. For another, tiny changes—wind speed, temperature—can eventually dramatically alter air movement, suddenly altering the turbulence once predicted. To make perfect forecasts, one would need a perfect picture of exactly what’s going on in the atmosphere at all times.

But increasing sophisticated applications of machine learning could allow scientists to get closer to knowing what’s going to happen when, says Murillo. And while brute, computational force can’t solve the turbulence problem, AI agents might give the effort a boost. OpenAI’s blockbuster announcement this fall that it had resolved the Navier-Stokes problem—equations that are the beginning of all turbulence models—suggests LLMs could help.
“Turbulence has been a problem only human minds could work on; as of this year, that's no longer true,” says Murillo.

news.summary_en:

paragraphs: One night in October, hackers staged one of the most unusual cyber attacks in history: cranking up the temperature in refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets across France and destroying millions of euros of food.

Hackers have targeted commercial fridges and freezers before, but never at this scale and never in the heart of Europe. The brazen attack left cyber professionals unsure as to who might have executed such a madcap operation. But French intelligence agencies found traces of Farsi and other clues in the digital trail pointing to an elite hacking unit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The unit allegedly behind the hack, Shahid Kaveh, was already well known to western intelligence agencies. Named after Mahmoud Kaveh, an Iranian commander who died during the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, it is one of several hacking units overseen by the Revolutionary Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command.

The group, which often goes by the online persona CyberAv3ngers, has a history of targeting critical infrastructure. In 2023 and 2024, it hacked Israeli-made industrial control devices inside water, manufacturing and transportation systems across several US states. Operational disruption was minimal, but the attackers left a message each time: “Every equipment ‘made in Israel’ is CyberAv3ngers legal target.”

State-backed Iranian hackers have rarely targeted Europe in this way, however. October’s hacks, experts say, mark an escalation in the Islamic republic’s cyber warfare strategy and a new willingness to hit European infrastructure.
“Iran has very clearly messaged that the global economy will be disrupted as a consequence of it being shut out from the world,” said Ellie Geranmayeh of the European Council on Foreign Relations.

While France and other European countries have largely stayed out of the US and Israel’s campaign against Iran, which started in February, the Islamic republic increasingly views all Nato countries as legitimate targets, she continued. “This is about sowing panic in Europe and increasing that global pain threshold.”
Similar attacks were staged this month against supermarkets in 10 other countries across Europe, though no group has yet been blamed.

Iran has denied any role in the freezer hacks, but France is seeking international arrest warrants for three Iranians allegedly involved: Hamid Reza Lashgarian, believed by US intelligence to be head of the Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command, and two Shahid Kaveh leaders, 37-year-old Mahdi Lashgarian and 35-year-old Reza Salarvand. Both Lashgarians were placed under US sanctions in 2024.
Often staffed with young engineers and software developers, the Revolutionary Guards’ cyber units have developed formidable skills in espionage and cyber warfare.

“Iran is a country of engineers, and people continue to underestimate its capabilities,” said Sanam Vakil, Middle East director at Chatham House think-tank. “It has a long history of successful cyber operations,” she added, noting that Iran had learnt through its own experience of cyber attacks, most notably the Stuxnet assault on its nuclear programme by the US and Israel in 2009.

French intelligence agencies have said the group used a Chinese-made scanning tool to scour the public internet for connected refrigeration units. Infrastructure linked to the group also conducted reconnaissance using Modbus, a digital language widely used to control industrial machinery — a technique Shahid Kaveh has employed since at least April, according to the authorities.

news.summary_en: The US Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule, effective around November 16, 2026, targeting remote access to high-end AI compute by Chinese entities at non-US data centers. paragraphs: Washington has spent years stopping advanced AI chips from physically reaching China. It turns out the chips never had to travel at all.

On Monday, the US Commerce Department issued a rule aimed at Chinese companies that tap high-end AI hardware sitting in data centers outside China. The move lands hardest on Southeast Asia, a region that has been building server farms at a brisk clip.
The rule comes from the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS. It is an interim final rule, with an effective date of approximately November 16, 2026.
Its core target is remote access. A Chinese firm does not need to own an Nvidia or AMD chip to use one. It can simply rent compute from a facility abroad and run its workloads over the internet.

The rule also reaches data centers directly. Any facility providing significant compute to Chinese entities needs a license and must carry out enhanced due diligence once it crosses a threshold of over 12 million aggregate TPP.
Operators get a 90-day compliance window after the rule takes effect. Those that miss it may face future restrictions.
There is one notable carve-out. US-headquartered operators are exempt from certain licensing requirements, though they must submit monthly compliance reports.

The rule is largely a response to the scandal around Nvidia and Megaspeed, a data center operator. Megaspeed spent at least $4.6 billion on Nvidia servers between 2023 and 2025.

The controversy centers on allegations that chips were diverted and that major Chinese clients, including Alibaba, gained remote access to compute. Those are allegations, not findings, but they were enough to push regulators into action.
Markets responded quickly. Shares of Southeast Asian companies linked to data centers fell after the announcement, with some dropping by as much as 20%.

news.author: Manuel Uth
news.content_snippet:
MIT researchers have developed a method that makes training AI climate models faster, cheaper, and more reliable. According to MIT News, these emulators now need only a fraction of the data typically required.

Normally, researchers rely on massive, physics-based climate simulations that take months to run a single scenario on supercomputers. Fast AI models for climate prediction can mimic these in seconds and help plan power grids, public health measures, and agriculture. But training them prev
news.summary_en: Researchers from MIT, ETH Zurich, and Imperial College London have developed a method to train AI climate emulators using synthetic data characterized by extreme environmental fluctuations, such as sudden CO2 spikes. This approach allows models to achieve high precision and robustness with only a single simulation run, significantly reducing computational demand.
paragraphs: MIT researchers have developed a method that makes training AI climate models faster, cheaper, and more reliable. According to MIT News, these emulators now need only a fraction of the data typically required.

Normally, researchers rely on massive, physics-based climate simulations that take months to run a single scenario on supercomputers. Fast AI models for climate prediction can mimic these in seconds and help plan power grids, public health measures, and agriculture. But training them previously required six to eight runs of those large simulations using evenly distributed, realistic future scenarios. That took so long the finished models were usually outdated, according to co-author Noelle Selin. They also often failed on unfamiliar situations.

An algorithm built by a team from MIT, ETH Zurich, and Imperial College London uses synthetic training data with extreme swings instead, like a sudden CO2 spike in 2050 or dropping methane in 2037. These targeted spikes help the AI understand the climate system far more precisely, according to lead author Christopher Womack. A single simulation run is enough for training, according to the team, and the AI reliably calculates the effects of local environmental policies too.

news.title: Exclusive: Meta and Amazon discuss ending Muse shopping bot blockade, as ads, search emerge as key issues
news.title_en: Exclusive: Meta and Amazon discuss ending Muse shopping bot blockade, as ads, search emerge as key issues
news.author: Sebastian Herrera
news.content_snippet:
Amazon and Meta Platforms are in ongoing discussions over a potential deal to connect Meta’s popular Muse AI agent to the e-commerce giant’s online store and end a blockade of the shopping bot imposed by Amazon two months ago.

The two tech giants have held talks on multiple occasions, and two major factors being negotiated are how the companies will handle search results and advertising in any deal, according to people familiar with the matter. Discussions are fluid, and it’s unclear if or how
news.summary_en: Meta Platforms and Amazon are negotiating the potential integration of Meta's Muse AI agent into Amazon's e-commerce platform, seeking to reverse a block imposed two months ago. The core tensions involve potential cannibalization of Amazon's advertising revenue and the risks of disintermediation between brands and their end consumers.
paragraphs: Amazon and Meta Platforms are in ongoing discussions over a potential deal to connect Meta’s popular Muse AI agent to the e-commerce giant’s online store and end a blockade of the shopping bot imposed by Amazon two months ago.

The two tech giants have held talks on multiple occasions, and two major factors being negotiated are how the companies will handle search results and advertising in any deal, according to people familiar with the matter. Discussions are fluid, and it’s unclear if or how soon an agreement will be struck. There are numerous issues, ranging from Amazon’s own AI shopping ambitions to how exactly Muse would connect to Amazon. A major threat Muse poses to Amazon is that, in theory, it would bypass advertisements on Amazon’s website, which are a large source of revenue for the retailer.

Amazon is worried about losing advertising revenue and about the quality of the product search results Muse would surface, and executives are also concerned that shopping agents like Muse will weaken the relationship Amazon has with consumers, the people said. Any deal between Amazon and Meta is expected to require sign-off from the CEOs of both companies, they said.

Meta and Amazon declined to comment. The negotiations are being closely followed because they have major implications for the future of online shopping and represent an important test case for how large corporations respond to the advent of AI agents. As agents like Muse become more widely used, companies like Amazon are scrambling to understand how the bots alter typical shopping patterns as well as the valued connections that brands and retailers have with consumers.

The talks are ongoing as Amazon prepares for another Black Friday and Cyber Monday, one of its most critical shopping periods of the year. This year, roughly half of holiday shoppers plan to use AI in some way to help make purchases, a National Retail Federation survey this month showed.

AI agents promise to bring major changes to many industries. Agentic shopping could total $190 billion to $385 billion in U.S. e-commerce spending by 2030, representing 10% to 20% of the total market, according to a 2025 report by Morgan Stanley. Analysts at JPMorgan have praised Muse as a powerful agent, recently writing that tens of millions of businesses could eventually use the tool.

Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse app from accessing its store in September, saying at the time that Muse’s access would violate its user agreements. Muse, which Meta released in the U.S. that month, is a personalized AI agent that users can name and have autonomously carry out tasks on their behalf, such as checking email, managing calendars and booking reservations. As of October, more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set up the app, making it Meta’s biggest consumer AI hit to date. Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg has said shopping is Muse’s top use case.

“We think that billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together,” Zuckerberg said last month in a call with analysts. “We’d like to create a large scale Muse network as quickly as possible.”

One of Amazon’s main concerns is how shopping agents such as Muse will affect its advertising business. Advertising has become a $68.6 billion business for Amazon, representing nearly 10% of its total yearly revenue. In October, Amazon Chief Executive Andy Jassy, while not naming Muse, tried to quell investor concern by saying few customers are buying with outside shopping agents because the experience is “still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly.”
Still, Jassy said this month at a Semafor conference that Amazon hadn’t ruled out letting outside shopping agents into its store, but that they would have to provide a “fair exchange of value.”

Aside from Meta, OpenAI launched its Dots personal AI agents in September, and startup Instinct’s personal assistant has also become a mainstream AI agent. Amazon has its own shopping agent for its website, dubbed “Alexa for shopping,” which Jassy said has been used by more than 400 million customers in the past year.

Meta and Amazon have partnered on e-commerce before. In 2023, the companies struck a deal that allowed Facebook and Instagram users to purchase Amazon products without leaving the apps. Meta makes money from ads it serves users on its apps, including for Amazon products, and Amazon earns revenue through the actual purchases. The partnership was made as TikTok expanded into U.S. e-commerce.

news.title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
news.title_en: AI is straining America’s open records systems
news.author: Rachel Courtland
news.content_snippet:
